en.title: Architecture and Settlement
en.summary: Architecture in Mithila, Vajji and Anga survives unevenly. Massive brick ramparts, stupas, monasteries, rock-cut shrines and temple fragments are visible; timber houses, thatch, fences, workshops and periodic markets are far less so. This chapter therefore joins architecture to settlement archaeology.

mai.title: वास्तुकला आ बसावट
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “वास्तुकला आ बसावट” विषयक वास्तु, वस्त्र, भोजन, चित्रकला, संगीत, रंगमंच, मेला आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृतिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Architecture as social history, not a catalogue of monuments
The alluvial plain as an architectural environment
Preservation bias: earth, timber and thatch versus brick and stone
Settlement archaeology and the problem of historical names

en.title: Dress, Textiles and Ornament
en.summary: Dress history in Mithila, Vajji and Anga survives through an unequal archive. Cloth normally decays, while stone beads, shell bangles, terracotta ornaments, production tools, sculpture and words endure. This chapter therefore reconstructs clothing and adornment by triangulating archaeology, art and text, with a chronology firewall against projecting later fashions or the modern reputation of Bhagalpur silk backward into periods for which continuity has not been demonstrated.

mai.title: पोशाक, वस्त्र आ आभूषण
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “पोशाक, वस्त्र आ आभूषण” विषयक वास्तु, वस्त्र, भोजन, चित्रकला, संगीत, रंगमंच, मेला आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृतिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Dress as material culture and social history
The preservation problem: cloth disappears, ornament survives
Fibres, fabrics and the danger of naming local production
Spinning as the archaeological doorway into textile production

en.title: Food History of Mithila, Vajji and Anga
en.summary: A history of food in Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot begin by copying a modern recipe list backward into antiquity. Food is unusually vulnerable to historical distortion because cooked dishes disappear almost completely, while modern regional cuisines are vivid and familiar.

mai.title: मिथिला, वज्जि आ अंगक भोजन-इतिहास
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मिथिला, वज्जि आ अंगक भोजन-इतिहास” विषयक वास्तु, वस्त्र, भोजन, चित्रकला, संगीत, रंगमंच, मेला आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृतिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Food history is an evidence problem before it is a cuisine story
The alluvial ecology behind the regional food system
Chirand as a regional comparator, not a substitute for Mithila
Rice: central crop, contested beginnings

en.title: Mithila Painting Before and Beyond the Modern Art Market
en.summary: Mithila painting presents a paradox for the social historian. The practice is repeatedly described as old, yet its most durable and datable corpus is overwhelmingly modern because the older media were intentionally temporary. Floor diagrams were renewed, mud-plastered walls were resurfaced, pigments faded, houses were rebuilt, and floods, earthquakes and poverty repeatedly altered domestic architecture. The result is a severe survival bias.

mai.title: आधुनिक कला-बजारसँ पहिने आ ओकर पार मिथिला चित्रकला
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “आधुनिक कला-बजारसँ पहिने आ ओकर पार मिथिला चित्रकला” विषयक वास्तु, वस्त्र, भोजन, चित्रकला, संगीत, रंगमंच, मेला आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृतिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Why the pre-market history is difficult to write
Painting was embedded in domestic space before it became a portable object
Aripan: temporary geometry and the problem of preservation
Kohbar painting and the nuptial chamber

en.title: Mithila Painting and the Twentieth-Century Cultural Economy
en.summary: Mithila painting entered a new historical regime in the twentieth century. The domestic ritual practice discussed in Chapter 47 did not suddenly begin when administrators, craft officials, collectors or museums noticed it. What changed was the social life of the image. A painted wall or floor was tied to a house, ceremony and cycle of renewal; a sheet of paper could be counted, priced, signed, packed, retailed, exhibited, collected and archived. This chapter therefore studies cultural economy rather than origins.

mai.title: मिथिला चित्रकला आ बीसम शताब्दीक सांस्कृतिक अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मिथिला चित्रकला आ बीसम शताब्दीक सांस्कृतिक अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक वास्तु, वस्त्र, भोजन, चित्रकला, संगीत, रंगमंच, मेला आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृतिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: The twentieth-century cultural economy is a second history, not the origin of the art
The 1934 earthquake created visibility through destruction
Archer’s photographs and 1949 article helped create a metropolitan art object
Independence changed the institutional setting of craft and rural art

en.title: Music, Song and Performance
en.summary: Music becomes historical evidence only when it is attached to a dateable setting: who performed, for whom, on what occasion, in what language, and through what medium. A song-text without a performance context is not the same thing as a sounded event; a living performance is not by itself proof that the same melody, instrumentation or social meaning existed centuries earlier. This chapter therefore treats music, song and performance as connected but separately testable histories across Mithila, Vajji and Anga.

mai.title: संगीत, गीत आ प्रदर्शन
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “संगीत, गीत आ प्रदर्शन” विषयक वास्तु, वस्त्र, भोजन, चित्रकला, संगीत, रंगमंच, मेला आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृतिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Performance history requires an event, a repertoire and a social setting
Sound is unusually vulnerable evidence
Pan-Indian music theory is a framework, not a regional transcript
Nanyadeva provides rare early evidence linking Mithila to written musicology

en.title: Theatre and Dramatic Cultures
en.summary: The history of theatre cannot be written from playbooks alone. A dramatic text preserves possible speech, songs, roles and sequences, but performance also requires bodies, voice, movement, music, costume, a place, an audience and a social occasion. For Mithila, Vajji and Anga the archive is therefore uneven: some periods preserve manuscripts but no witnessed staging; others preserve living performance with uncertain antiquity; still others leave only literary references to actors or entertainment.

mai.title: रंगमंच आ नाट्य-संस्कृति
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “रंगमंच आ नाट्य-संस्कृति” विषयक वास्तु, वस्त्र, भोजन, चित्रकला, संगीत, रंगमंच, मेला आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृतिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Theatre is an event before it is a text
Dramatic evidence survives in unequal layers
The Nāṭyaśāstra provides concepts, not a local transcript
Jyotiriśvara’s Dhūrtasamāgama is a crucial early dramatic witness

en.title: Fairs, Markets and Public Culture
en.summary: A weekly haat, an annual mela and an everyday bazaar were not interchangeable institutions. Their calendars, catchment areas and social expectations differed. A haat concentrated ordinary exchange on one or two days and linked surrounding villages to itinerant traders, cultivators and petty retailers. A mela usually gathered a much larger and more heterogeneous public around a ritual date, shrine, river crossing, seasonal need or established custom.

mai.title: मेला, बजार आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृति
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मेला, बजार आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृति” विषयक वास्तु, वस्त्र, भोजन, चित्रकला, संगीत, रंगमंच, मेला आ सार्वजनिक संस्कृतिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Periodic exchange created a different kind of public space
Markets were also theatres of information
The archive overrepresents spectacular fairs
Archaeology can identify exchange without identifying a mela
